title: Restaurant voicemail greeting examples for busy owners
seoTitle: Restaurant voicemail greeting examples for busy owners
description: Use these restaurant voicemail greeting examples, plus after-hours scripts and setup tips, to create a cleaner guest experience.
question: What should I say in a restaurant voicemail greeting?
answer: A good restaurant voicemail greeting should say who you are, when you are open, and what the caller should do next. Keep it short, clear, and useful: mention hours, invite pickup orders or questions during business hours, and give an alternate way to reach you for urgent matters. If you want fewer missed calls, use a phone host like ROAL during open hours and a simple voicemail after hours.
summary: You’ll know how to write a clear voicemail greeting, when to use it, and how to turn missed calls into better guest follow-up.
intro:
A restaurant voicemail greeting should be short, clear, and helpful. It should tell callers where they reached, when you are open, and what to do next if you cannot answer.

For a busy pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant, the best greeting is the one that saves time for guests and staff. It should fit your hours, your pickup flow, and your after-hours routine without sounding stiff.

sections.h2: What should a restaurant voicemail greeting say?
sections.body:
A good restaurant voicemail greeting should answer the caller’s first three questions fast: did I reach the right place, are you open, and what should I do now? Keep it simple. If the message is too long, people hang up before leaving a name or number.

Use this basic structure:
1. Greet the caller and name the restaurant.
2. Say whether you are open or closed.
3. Tell them what to leave in the message.
4. Give one useful next step, like calling back during business hours or checking your website.

Here is a plain example you can use:
"Thanks for calling Maria’s Pizza. We’re currently closed. Please leave your name, number, and a short message, and we’ll get back to you during our next business hours. For pickup orders and menu questions, please call back when we’re open."

If you take pickup orders by phone, mention that clearly. If you get a lot of catering or reservation calls, say so too. The goal is not to sound fancy. The goal is to help the guest and reduce repeat calls.

sections.h2: Can you use one voicemail greeting for open and closed hours?
sections.body:
You can, but it is usually better to use different messages for open hours and after hours. A caller who reaches voicemail at 2 p.m. expects something different from someone calling at 10:30 p.m. after dinner rush.

Here is a simple split:
- **Open hours message:** explains that the restaurant is busy or unavailable right now, but open.
- **Closed hours message:** explains that you are closed and when to call back.

Example open-hours script:
"Thanks for calling Tony’s Deli. We’re open now, but we can’t take your call right this second. Please leave your name and number, and we’ll call you back as soon as we can. If you’re calling about a pickup order, please include what you’d like and when you need it."

Example after-hours script:
"Thanks for calling Tony’s Deli. We’re closed right now. Please leave your name, number, and message, and we’ll return your call during business hours. For menu questions, pickup orders, or hours, please call us back when we open."

If you use [after-hours phone message examples](/blog/after-hours-message-examples), keep the wording tight and practical. A short message is easier to hear over a loud parking lot, a car speaker, or a late-night call.

sections.h2: Which voicemail script works best for pickup and delivery callers?
sections.body:
If most of your calls are pickup or delivery orders, your voicemail should make that clear. People often call because they want food fast, not because they want a long message.

Try this structure for a voicemail greeting focused on orders:
- Say the restaurant name.
- Tell callers whether ordering is available by voicemail or not.
- Ask for the exact details you need.
- Set expectations for response time.

Example script:
"Thanks for calling Green Garden. We’re unable to take your call right now. If you want to place a pickup or delivery order, please leave your name, phone number, what you’d like, and the time you need it. We’ll call you back as soon as possible."

If you want to reduce missed orders instead of relying on voicemail, a phone host like ROAL can answer calls, take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It can also collect the caller’s name, phone number, and ready time. That matters when the dinner rush starts and nobody has time to return voicemail messages one by one.

Quick checklist for an order-focused voicemail:
- Restaurant name is clear.
- Caller knows whether you can take orders by voicemail.
- Name and phone number are requested.
- Order details are requested.
- No card numbers are requested.

sections.h2: How do I keep voicemail from sounding rude or confusing?
sections.body:
A voicemail greeting should sound calm, not cold. Many guests call because they are hungry, driving, or multitasking. A harsh message makes a simple call feel harder than it needs to be.

Use warm, plain language. Avoid lines like "your call is important to us" if that does not sound like your place. A neighborhood spot can sound like a neighborhood spot.

Use this tone guide:
| Do say | Avoid saying |
|---|---|
| “Thanks for calling” | “You have reached the office of...” |
| “Please leave your name and number” | “Your message will be monitored” |
| “We’ll call you back during business hours” | “Your call will be returned in a timely manner” |
| “For pickup orders, call back when we’re open” | Long explanations |

A better voicemail is often just 15 to 25 seconds. That is enough for the caller to understand the next step. If you have several locations, keep each location’s greeting specific so guests do not get lost. ROAL does this by giving each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, but your voicemail should still sound like the right store if someone reaches it.

If you need a simple line to read aloud, try: "Thanks for calling. Please leave your name, number, and what you need, and we’ll follow up during business hours."

sections.h2: What voicemail greeting should I use for common restaurant situations?
sections.body:
Different call types need different wording. A reservation call is not the same as a complaint, and a catering request is not the same as a late-night order. If your voicemail is too broad, you lose context.

Here are useful examples you can swap for your own details:

| Situation | Example voicemail line |
|---|---|
| Closed for the night | “We’re closed now. Please leave your name, number, and message, and we’ll call you back tomorrow.” |
| Busy lunch rush | “We’re helping guests in the restaurant right now. Please leave your name and number, and we’ll return your call as soon as we can.” |
| Pickup orders | “If you want to place a pickup order, leave your name, phone number, and what you’d like.” |
| Reservations | “For reservation requests, leave your name, number, party size, and requested time.” |
| Catering | “For catering inquiries, please leave your name, phone number, date, and event details.” |
| Allergy questions | “For allergy-sensitive questions, leave a detailed message and we’ll have staff follow up.” |

This is also where a phone host can help during business hours. ROAL can hand off allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering calls, and manager requests to staff with a summary, which keeps voicemail from becoming the only backup plan.

A practical tip: put the most common reason people call first. If most of your callers ask about hours and pickup, say that before anything else. If catering is important to your business, mention that too.

sections.h2: How do I set up voicemail and call forwarding without making it messy?
sections.body:
Voicemail works best when it is part of a simple call plan, not the whole plan. Many restaurants forward their main number when they are busy or closed, then let voicemail catch the overflow. The exact forwarding codes depend on your carrier or phone system, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

General patterns many owners use:
- Some landlines and carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off.
- On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off.
- **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls.
- **67*number# often forwards busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in a web portal.

A simple setup flow:
1. Choose where calls go during busy periods.
2. Record a short voicemail greeting.
3. Test forwarding with one real or test call.
4. Make sure the caller hears the correct message.
5. Check that voicemail messages reach the right person.

If you want a cleaner setup, ROAL can answer the restaurant’s phone, take orders from the live menu, and send questions it cannot answer to an inbox. The owner answers once, and the host learns it from then on. That can reduce how often callers reach voicemail in the first place.

For forwarding details by carrier, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should I do if voicemail is costing me orders?
sections.body:
If callers are landing in voicemail during the hours you are open, treat that as a guest-experience problem, not just a phone problem. A missed call can turn into a lost pickup order, a missed catering lead, or a frustrated guest who calls a different place.

Start with this quick audit:
1. Call your own number at lunch, dinner, and after hours.
2. Listen to the greeting from a guest’s point of view.
3. Check whether the message says the right hours.
4. Make sure someone can actually listen to voicemail quickly.
5. Decide which calls should go to staff and which should go to voicemail.

Here is a worked example you can plug your own numbers into. Say your average pickup order is $28. If voicemail causes even a few callers to hang up and place that order somewhere else, the lost revenue adds up fast over a week. Use your own average order amount and your own call volume to judge whether the current setup is working.

If you are comparing options, [AI phone host vs voicemail](/compare/voicemail) is a useful place to start. ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, and no per-minute fee, so you can compare it against voicemail plus the cost of missed calls in a straightforward way.

Want to try a cleaner phone setup? [build a free test host from your website](/try) and see how it handles your menu, hours, and pickup calls.

takeaways: Keep your voicemail short, warm, and specific to your restaurant.
Mention hours, name, number, and the exact next step callers should take.
Use separate wording for open-hours and after-hours calls when possible.
If voicemail is causing missed orders, consider a phone host during business hours and voicemail after hours.
Test your greeting by calling your own number from a guest’s point of view.

faq.q: What is the best voicemail greeting for a restaurant?
faq.a: The best restaurant voicemail greeting is short and practical. It should say the restaurant name, whether you are open or closed, and what details the caller should leave. A simple message that asks for name, number, and reason for calling is usually enough.

faq.q: Should a restaurant voicemail say the menu or hours?
faq.a: It should mention hours if callers may be reaching you after hours, but it should not try to say too much. If guests frequently ask about menu items or hours, keep those details in the greeting or direct them to call back during business hours. A long voicemail is easy to skip over.

faq.q: Can a restaurant take orders through voicemail?
faq.a: You can ask callers to leave order details in voicemail, but voicemail is not a great order-taking tool. Guests may speak too fast, forget details, or hang up before leaving enough information. A phone host is better for live order taking, and voicemail is better as a backup.

faq.q: How long should a restaurant voicemail greeting be?
faq.a: Aim for about 15 to 25 seconds. That is usually enough time to say the restaurant name, hours or closure status, and the next step. Shorter is better because callers often listen in a noisy car or while they are in a hurry.
